ai.base_rate_used: The scenario page's base rate: 0 downgrades in 36 recorded S&P actions on EU sovereigns with a stable outlook going in (0%). With an assumed 156 scheduled reviews, 0% is only a lower bound. Agencies almost always move the outlook to negative before they cut, so I start near zero and leave a small tail for a direct cut.

factors.text: Going in, the outlook was stable. In the reference class S&P never cut from a stable outlook (0 of 36). The usual sequence is an outlook change first and a cut at a later review, so the realistic bad outcome today is 'affirmed, outlook to negative', which resolves NO.

Market stress has risen sharply. The OAT-Bund spread averaged 147.4 bp in October against 96.7 bp in September, and the France 10-year averaged 4.89% against 4.44%. Rising borrowing costs feed straight into the debt path that S&P scores. Caveat: this is a degraded monthly series and the badge says untested.

The budget is fragile. Market odds of a 2027 budget by 31 December are 43.5% on Polymarket and 39.0% on Kalshi, and both fell this week. The HCFP calls the 1.0% growth assumption optimistic and judges the 2027 deficit reduction too slow. This is the kind of political risk that points to a negative outlook rather than an immediate cut. Moody's affirmed with a negative outlook on 23 Oct, so S&P faces no peer pressure from a fresh cut.

ai.what_would_change_view: The S&P publication itself, due after the market close today, settles the question. Before then, only one thing would move me materially toward YES: a government collapse on a censure motion, or a formal shift to a special law before the decision. Neither appears in the facts.
ai.most_likely_wrong: The crowd at 5.5% and my 5% may share the same mistake: assuming S&P follows its usual outlook-first sequence. A spread that widened by about 50 bp in a month and a stalled budget could push S&P to cut directly, as agencies sometimes do when market access deteriorates fast. The prediction-market signal carries the tested_no_lead badge, so its agreement with me adds little comfort.

ai.base_rate_used: The scenario page's base rate is 19 of 21 budgets promulgated by 31 December (90.5%), for French budget laws from 2006 to 2026. That rate is dominated by years when the government had a majority. The page shows the subset since June 2022, when the government lost its majority, separately but gives no figure for it. In that period the last two cycles ended in a special law rather than a budget, the December 2025 one among them (the special_law analog). So I start well below 90.5%, from the minority-government record, which looks closer to a coin flip.

factors.text: Structure: a minority government since the 2024 dissolution has needed either Article 49.3 or a special law to finish each budget, and the recent cycles fell back on a special law. The 90.5% base rate comes from a regime that no longer exists.

The bills ask for about 54 billion euros of consolidation, including a freeze of basic pensions except the lowest and of civil-service pay. The HCFP calls the 1.0% growth assumption optimistic. Measures this unpopular, months before a presidential election, make a non-censure deal with the PS or LR harder to get. The October jump in the OAT-Bund spread to 147.4 bp from 96.7 bp shows markets already pricing political strain.

Routes to a YES still exist. Kalshi puts 58.0% on Article 49.3 being used on the budget in 2026, so the government seems ready to force the text through. The Article 47 ordinance route opens after the 10 Dec deadline. But it has never been used under the Fifth Republic and would invite a constitutional fight, so I give it little weight. Budget markets sit at 43.5% (Polymarket) and 39.0% (Kalshi) and are drifting down. Prediction-market series carry a tested_no_lead badge, so I use them only as a cross-check, not as a guide.

ai.what_would_change_view: I would move up if the PS or LR publicly commits not to vote censure on a 49.3 text, or if a joint committee (CMP) agreement lands in mid-December. I would also move up if the government signals clearly after 10 Dec that it will use Article 47, which would put the ordinance branch in play. I would move down if a special law is tabled, as in the 2024 and 2025 pattern, or if a censure motion starts gathering PS votes.
ai.most_likely_wrong: The shared mistake may be everyone, me included, anchoring on the last two years' special-law outcome. The government could get a 49.3 text through a censure vote with a quiet PS abstention, as happened in earlier minority years. In that case the 35% on adoption is too low and the markets near 40% are too pessimistic. A second risk is that the government breaks precedent and uses an Article 47 ordinance after 10 Dec.

ai.base_rate_used: The scenario page's base rate (final-poll leader won 4 of 4 run-offs; RMS poll error 5.78 pp) applies to final polls taken just before the vote. We are about five months out, and the snapshot has no run-off polls to apply it to, so it gives no usable number. As a last resort I start from market prices: Le Pen 44.2% on Polymarket and 45.0% on Kalshi, plus Bardella 1.2%, which puts the RN at about 45%.

factors.text: The fiscal and budget backdrop helps an anti-establishment candidate. Markets give only 43.5% (Polymarket) and 39.0% (Kalshi) to a budget being in place by year-end. The HCFP calls the growth assumption optimistic and expects debt to keep rising. The OAT-Bund spread widened to 147.4 bp in October from 96.7 bp in September. A visible failure to govern tends to feed the RN vote.

The centre-right field is starting to concentrate. Lisnard is at 23.9% on Polymarket and 27.0% on Kalshi, both up 1.0 pp, and Philippe rose to 5.7%. If one centre-right candidate gathers the vote, the RN would likely face a stronger opponent in the second round.

Almost all of the RN's market odds sit on one person: Le Pen at 44.2% against Bardella at 1.2%. That only makes sense if markets treat her ineligibility case as settled in her favour. If she is barred late, the RN probably does not keep all of her odds when it switches to Bardella.

ai.what_would_change_view: I would move toward a higher RN probability if published head-to-head second-round polls show the RN ahead of the leading centre-right candidate by more than the 5.78 pp final-poll error, or if the 2027 budget fails and the government falls in December. I would move lower if the centre-right settles on a single candidate (others withdrawing, or the parrainage counts in March 2027), or if a ruling on Le Pen's eligibility forces a late switch to Bardella.
ai.most_likely_wrong: I end up close to the market price, so I share whatever mistake the market is making. The evidence badges give little ground to second-guess it: the poll-versus-market gap is tested_no_lead and pollster herding is untested. Final polls have picked the winner, but this vote is five months away. A shock such as an eligibility ruling, a government falling, or a candidate withdrawing could move the outcome further than markets now allow, in either direction.

ai.base_rate_used: The scenario page has no computed base rate; em-macro records no Brazilian fiscal-target revisions. I start instead from Brazil's own record as context: the government cut a target it had set itself in July 2015 and in April 2024. Both cuts came mid-year or through the next year's guidelines bill, not in the first quarter. I also note that the tolerance band and exclusions give a cheaper way out than a formal cut. Start: about 70% that the target and rule survive to 31 March.

factors.text: The arithmetic is under strain. IFI projects an effective surplus of only R$18.6 billion (0.1% of GDP), against the government's target-counted R$83.4 billion. In IFI's scenario the counted result is R$0.9 billion, below even the lower tolerance bound, so about R$35.7 billion would need freezing. Focus puts the 2027 primary balance median at -0.4% of GDP. A target the market already doubts is easier to rewrite once a new term starts on 5 January.

The Senate approved the fiscal plan, and the government still claims formal compliance at 0.6% of GDP. That makes 'kept on paper, met through exclusions or one-offs' the path of least resistance before 31 March. That path resolves YES, and it is cheaper politically than sending a bill to a divided lower house.

Markets are pricing fiscal slippage. Over the week USD/BRL PTAX rose 4.89%, the DI Jan-29 proxy rose 39 bp and the longest fixed-rate bond rose 27 bp. These come after the post-run-off repricing. Selling pressure like this can either force a credibility gesture or signal that insiders expect loosening. The DI data are degraded proxies.

ai.what_would_change_view: I would move toward NO if a PLN or PLP to change the target or LC 200/2023 limits is sent, or if ministers publicly question the 0.5% target. A new finance minister in January who signals a rewrite would do the same, as would a December PLOA vote with new carve-outs plus talk of revising the target. I would move toward YES if the PLOA is voted around 17 December without new exclusions, a framework-keeping finance minister is named, and the Focus 2027 primary median moves toward the target.
ai.most_likely_wrong: A re-elected government at the start of a new term may decide to reset the target early, in January to March, to avoid a costly freeze. I may be wrong to assume that historical cuts came mid-year: a new-term finance team has both the motive and the political capital to act quickly. The crowd's risk is the reverse: the sharp BRL and DI selloff may be treating 'exclusions' and 'target cut' as the same thing. Leveraged funds were still at an extreme 99.4 percentile BRL long as of 17 November, but that positioning badge is tested_no_lead, and the Focus fiscal series is untested, so neither should carry much weight.

rows.note: Morena wins the most seats: implied by every branch except a large loss

rows.question: Mexican Chamber of Deputies election winner?: Morena
rows.note: same: the party with most seats

problems: number 87 is not a snapshot value
ai.base_rate_used: The scenario page's computed base rate (final-poll leader won 3 of 3 Mexican midterms; RMS poll error 4.12 pp) answers a different question: who comes first, not whether the coalition clears two-thirds. No computed rate exists for keeping a supermajority, so I start from the page's midterm context instead. In that small reference class (2009, 2015, 2021), the 2021 case is the only one where the governing coalition went in with two-thirds, and it kept its majority but lost the two-thirds. My starting point is therefore well below even odds, about one in three.

factors.text: Two-thirds is a high bar. The page's signposts say it needs roughly a 55% coalition vote share plus favourable over-representation rulings from the INE, which were already disputed in 2024. Midterms historically trim the governing side, and 2021 is the direct precedent: the majority was kept and two-thirds was lost.

Morena's dominance is not in doubt. Polymarket gives 88.3% and Kalshi 86.0% that it wins the most seats, and PAN is a distant second, so the losing-majority branch is small. These markets do not price the two-thirds line, and prediction-market series carry a tested_no_lead badge, so they set a floor for the majority branch rather than informing the supermajority question.

The economic backdrop going into the campaign is soft. The 2027 package lowers consolidation ambition, with a 3.9% RFSP deficit against the 3.5% planned in April. Pemex is still a fiscal drag, and USMCA uncertainty and new USTR labour cases weigh on investment. This argues mildly against an expanded mandate, though Mexican voters have so far not punished Morena for weak growth.

ai.what_would_change_view: Polls putting the coalition consistently above 55% of the vote, or an INE ruling on coalition over-representation that repeats the 2024 interpretation, would push me towards even odds. Coalition polls drifting toward 45%, or PAN-PRI-MC alliances in key districts, would push me lower. Candidate registration in January 2027 is the first hard signpost.
ai.most_likely_wrong: I may be underweighting how the over-representation rules and coalition seat-splitting turn a mid-50s vote share into two-thirds of seats, as they did in 2024. If opposition fragmentation persists, a midterm dip in votes may cost the coalition far fewer seats than the 2021 precedent implies. The crowd's shared error is to read the roughly 87% 'Morena wins most seats' prices as reassurance. Nothing liquid prices the two-thirds line, and in 2024 that line moved MXN −3.5% on day 1 and −7.2% by day 5, even though the presidential poll margin was never in doubt.

rows.question: Which USMCA outcomes will occur in 2026?: Trilateral revised deal

ai.base_rate_used: The scenario page has no computed base rate: this is the agreement's first review cycle, and em-macro has no trade-agreement events. I start instead from the closest market prices. These are only related, because they cover 2026 rather than the 1 Jul 2027 deadline: Kalshi gives a formal 16-year extension in 2026 4.0%, and Polymarket gives 'USMCA extended in 2026' 2.9%. I then allow a little extra room for the 2027 joint review itself.

factors.text: The US is still using USMCA's labour mechanism against Mexico rather than winding disputes down. USTR asked Mexico to review alleged denial of workers' rights at Industrias FG on 13 Nov and at Polygroup on 19 Nov. Ambassador Greer is publicly defending tariffs as a long-term policy. This does not look like an administration ready to sign a clean 16-year renewal.

Markets see a US withdrawal notice in 2026 (13.0%) as more likely than a formal 16-year extension (4.0%) or a trilateral revised deal (5.0%). Under the treaty, missing the 2026 extension means yearly reviews, so 'no extension, keep reviewing' is the default path.

The question window runs to 1 Jul 2027, not 31 Dec 2026. A USTR public consultation is expected around February 2027, and a deal could be traded for Mexican concessions at the 2027 review. That leaves more room than the 2026 markets price. Mexico's government is also politically stable, and the IMF has reaffirmed its credit line, so Mexico can negotiate.

ai.what_would_change_view: I would move up if USTR's 2027 consultation report recommends extension, if US tariffs on Mexican goods are cut, or if a trilateral revised text is announced. I would move down if the US proposes separate US-Mexico and US-Canada texts, if officials describe withdrawal as leverage, or if more labour-mechanism cases cluster ahead of the review.
ai.most_likely_wrong: The crowd and I may both be anchoring on the 2026 review's failure. A US administration that wants a headline 'win' could swap a quick 16-year extension for concessions on rules of origin or China content at the July 2027 review. The 2026 markets would miss that, and the evidence badges say prediction-market prices (pm., ks.) have shown no lead anyway.
